# AgentBisect `git bisect` for agent behavior. Give it a failing agent run (or just a known-good and known-bad commit). It finds the commit that broke the behavior, explains why that commit was written, and proves the culprit by reverting it. Built for neatHack (Oct 10, 2026). Business case: [AgentBisect financial model on CFO.ai](https://cfo.ai/s/nx6S-5QNKtJFVkRp) (spreadsheet copy: [`evidence/cfo-ai/`](evidence/cfo-ai/)). > Every figure below is copied from a file in `evidence/` (final re-run: [`evidence/rerun3-summary.md`](evidence/rerun3-summary.md)). > Open the HTML reports with `open evidence/report-.html`; `evidence/dogfooding.md` covers using AgentBisect on its own build. ## What it is Agents regress in ways unit tests do not catch: a refactor changes the unit of a refund amount, a "helpful" change makes the agent cancel orders nobody asked to cancel, a new tool schema quietly doubles token spend. `git bisect` can find the commit, but it needs a deterministic good/bad test, and an LLM agent gives you a noisy one. AgentBisect supplies that test. It runs the target repo's eval suite at each commit it probes, in an isolated git worktree, with repeats and a calibrated baseline so a flaky run is not mistaken for a regression. Then it bisects. The demo target is [`support-agent-demo`](https://github.com/jaxsonsprinkles/support-agent-demo): a customer-support agent (pinned Haiku) with mocked tools, 24 eval cases at HEAD (18 exist at the good commit), and a seeded history of regressions written by a separate coding-agent session. ## How it works 1. **Intake.** Start from a neatlogs trace, a neatlogs detection, or a GitHub issue. Intake maps it to an eval case, finds a known-good commit (an earlier passing run of the same case), and records a `RegressionSpec`. 2. **Failure signatures.** At the bad end, every distinct failing check (for example `call_args:issue_refund.amount`, `must_not_call`, `budget:tokens@order_status`) becomes its own *signature*, and each is bisected separately. One range can hide several regressions; bisecting "the suite fails" would blame whichever commit lands last. A signature that also fails at the good end is a known pre-existing failure, and AgentBisect refuses to bisect it instead of inventing a culprit. 3. **Plain bisect.** Classic binary search over `git rev-list --first-parent`, with a monotonic probe after convergence that flags "multiple regressions likely" when the history is not clean good-then-bad. 4. **Smart (weighted) bisect.** A planner ranks the commits in range by how likely each is to be the culprit, then picks the next commit by weighted bisection (split the probability mass, not the commit count) and falls back to plain when the ranking is uninformative. Signals, in order: - **Span divergence**: where the bad run first differs from a good run (a different tool, different arguments, an extra step). See [span divergence](#span-divergence-and-the-fixture-fallback). - **Code impact**: `entire graph impact` finds which commits touched the code behind the divergent tool. - **Entire intent**: each candidate's [Entire](https://entire.io) checkpoint (the prompt and reasoning of the coding session that wrote it). Commits that were *meant* to change the failing area rank higher. 5. **Median budget checks.** Token and step regressions are judged against a per-case **median** from a one-time calibration run at the good commit (`agentbisect calibrate`), never recalibrated mid-investigation. A run is over budget past 1.5x the case median. Medians, not means, so one slow sample does not move the line. 6. **Verifier (revert test).** The culp ... [6742 characters truncated] ... : step 1: bad run made an extra step search_help ``` The fixture is the tool-call sequence of case `os1` ("Where is order 1042?") at `1b40b27` and `0ecffc0`, taken from real `python -m evals run --json` output (Haiku through the llm-proxy). It is always labelled as a fixture, never presented as live neatlogs data. The bad commit is the tip of the range, so the fixture shows where behavior changed (an extra `search_help` step), not which commit caused it. It contains tool-call spans only; model-call spans are not in the runner's report. `agentbisect.fixtures.FixtureDirSource` plugs into the same `TraceSource` interface as the live source, and `--bundle OUT.json` writes the single-file form that `--fixtures` accepts. `record_pair` records new fixtures from two eval reports. ## Next steps These are the next steps for what we're going to tackle next with AgentBisect. Each one comes from something the evidence showed us. - **Unblock neatlogs span divergence.** Multi-span traces currently dead-letter (`finalizationStatus: "dlq"`, `spansCount: 0`), even for a bare two-span script with no model calls, and the SDK reports zero export failures. The trace ids are in [`evidence/neatlogs-dlq-report.md`](evidence/neatlogs-dlq-report.md). Once traces finalize, we'll run the planner on live span divergence instead of the recorded fixture (the final re-run ranked on code impact and checkpoint intent only), and verify `NeatlogsCliSource.spans` against the real span shape, since it was written against the documented CLI. - **Make token-budget signatures reliable.** Every token regression (a new tool schema, an extra "verify with search" rule) inflates every category, so a per-category budget signature tends to blame whichever commit crosses 1.5x last, and its revert test can fail with "multiple regressions likely". Behavioural signatures (wrong arguments, forbidden tool calls) are already far more reliable. We'll attribute token growth per commit rather than per threshold crossing; a tool-count signal for token signatures is on an unmerged branch. Per-signature outcomes are in `evidence/rerun3-summary.md` (4 of 6 correct on the final re-run). - **Make smart bisect cheaper on budget signatures.** It already uses fewer eval rounds than plain on behavioural signatures (18 vs 24, 3 vs 4), but more on budget signatures (96 vs 84, 60 vs 54). We'll improve the ranking there, and repeat the planner-context saving on more than one investigation and range. - **Tighten the noisy "bad" judgement.** Haiku at non-zero temperature (the proxy cannot set it) is stochastic. Repeats, medians and a confidence band reduce that noise; we want to cut it further, and keep labelling low-confidence culprits as such. - **Measure context savings properly.** The current token counts are bytes/4 estimates, and the "without graph" side is an estimate rather than a second run. We'll replace both with real token counts from actual runs. - **Broaden the Fixer and Verifier evidence.** So far it is one run per configuration, one culprit (R3), six runs in total, about $0.9 of model calls, and the one VERIFIED result is an eval-expectation update, not a code fix. We'll run more culprits and more samples, and get a real code fix through the Verifier. - **Make eval-expectation edits safer.** The Fixer's checks run the fix commit's own cases file, so an edited expectation is what they see; the Verifier flags the change rather than re-running against the old expectation. We'll re-check against the original expectations too, so a wrong "deliberate contract change" judgement cannot pass quietly. Until then, a person should read the flagged list. - **Extend the Fixer and Verifier to budget regressions.** They have only been exercised on a behavioural signature, and the Verifier ignores `budget:*` flags in regression and held-out checks unless the target is itself a budget signature. - **Try more than one target repo.** Everything has run against `support-agent-demo`. The eval contract is generic, so next we'll point AgentBisect at other agent repos. ## Repository map | Path | What | |---|---| | `agentbisect/intake.py` | trace/detection/issue intake, `TraceSource` (neatlogs CLI and fixture sources) | | `agentbisect/runner.py`, `baseline.py` | isolated eval runs, repeats, caching, median-token baseline | | `agentbisect/signature.py`, `bisect.py`, `planner.py` | failure signatures, plain and weighted bisect, ranking | | `agentbisect/culprit.py`, `verify.py` | Entire intent + diff + divergence, revert test | | `agentbisect/fixtures.py`, `fixtures/` | recorded good/bad trace pair for the divergence step | | `agentbisect/llm_proxy.py` | Anthropic-compatible proxy over your `claude` login | | `evidence/` | reports and re-run summaries | | `docs/demo-script.md`, `docs/storyboard.md` | 3-minute demo narration and shot list | | `hackathon.md`, `BUILD_LOG.md`, `ROLES.md` | build log, roles and pinning rules | vercel not found /Users/jaxson/.bun/bin/bun /opt/homebrew/bin/node

5. **Median budget checks.** Token and step regressions are judged against a per-case **median** from a one-time calibration run at the good commit (`agentbisect calibrate`), never recalibrated mid-investigation. A run is over budget past 1.5x the case median. Medians, not means, so one slow sample does not move the line.
6. **Verifier (revert test).** The culprit is only reported with confidence if reverting it at the bad end flips the signature from failing to passing (before and after pass rates are recorded). Revert conflicts, partial reverts and unbuildable trees lower confidence or end as `inconclusive`.
7. **Explain.** The culprit report quotes the Entire checkpoint (why the commit was written), the semantic diff, and the first span divergence, so the answer is "this commit, written to do X, causes Y", not just a SHA.
8. **Fixer.** A fresh agent that sees only the culprit diff, the stated intent, and the failing evidence (never the planted-regression metadata) proposes a fix that keeps the intent, up to 3 attempts. An intent check runs inside the Fixer, so "revert the culprit" does not pass. Where the culprit *deliberately* changed a contract and the eval expectations are stale, the Fixer may update those expectations, narrowly and only for cases sharing the target's check; every such change is recorded and flagged "human review required". `report --open-pr` and `fix --open-draft-pr` are dry runs by default and push nothing without explicit confirmation.
9. **Fix Verifier.** `agentbisect verify-fix` re-checks the fix commit on four counts: the target signature no longer reproduces, the regression suite still passes, held-out cases pass (the fix is not overfit), and a pinned intent judge says the culprit's intent survives. Any failure is NOT VERIFIED; a judge outage or missing held-out cases is inconclusive, never a pass.

Roles, model pins and isolation rules are in [`ROLES.md`](ROLES.md). The agent and judge models are pinned and recorded in every result, and results produced under different pins are never mixed.

### Fixer and Verifier: live results

Run six times live on the R3 refund-amount culprit `b0be626` ([`evidence/fix-demo/README.md`](evidence/fix-demo/README.md)). Run 6 is **VERIFIED**: target pass, regression 13/13, held-out 1.00 (with 1 held-out expectation change), intent judge pass. Read what the fix is: **it changes no code.** The culprit deliberately moved `issue_refund` to integer cents, so the eval expectations were stale; the fix updates 4 eval expectations (rw1-rw3 target, rw4 held-out), all flagged for human review. A person should confirm that is the intended resolution.

The earlier runs are the interesting part: the Fixer reverted the culprit and passed its own checks (the intent judge caught it), frozen evals made any fix impossible, and two bugs in our own guards turned up live. Each led to a change. 326 tests pass.

## Setup

Requirements: Python 3.11 to 3.13 (the neatlogs SDK does not support 3.14), [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), `git`, and for the full pipeline the `entire` CLI with the `graph` plugin.

```bash
uv sync
cp .env.example .env     # NEATLOGS_API_KEY, NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID, ...
uv run pytest -q         # fake executors and throwaway git repos; no model or network calls
```

The target repo needs `evals/cases.jsonl` and the eval CLI contract (`python -m evals run --json --isolate ...`, schema version 1) described in the `support-agent-demo` repo. Clone it next to this one.

Optional pieces:

- **neatlogs CLI** (`npm i -g --prefix ~/.local/neatlogs-cli neatlogs-cli`) for live trace intake, after a one-time `auth login --device`. See `hackathon.md`.
- **Entire** (`entire enable` in the target repo; `entire plugin install graph`) for checkpoint intent and code impact. Without it the planner falls back to commit messages and plain bisect.
- **LLM backend.** Either set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or run on your own logged-in `claude` CLI with `--llm-proxy auto` (personal use, your own login only; see `ROLES.md`). The proxy cannot set temperature, so repeats absorb the extra noise.

## Usage

```bash
# 1. Calibrate the token baseline once, at the known-good commit
uv run agentbisect calibrate --repo ../support-agent-demo --good 1b40b27 --llm-proxy auto

# 2. Investigate from a bad trace (or --detection ID, or --issue URL)

<!-- boardui:rules:start -->
# BoardUI design rules

This project uses BoardUI (React + Tailwind CSS v4, source-owned components under `components/`). These rules always apply when writing UI code. MCP tools are on demand; these rules are not optional context.

## Components first

- Before hand-building any UI element, check for an installed BoardUI component under `components/base/` and `components/application/`, and prefer it.
- Missing a component? Install it (BoardUI MCP `install_components`, or `npx boardui@latest add <name>`) instead of writing a lookalike.
- Import through the `@/` alias, e.g. `import { Button } from "@/components/base/buttons/button"`.

## Color: semantic tokens only

- Never use raw palette classes (`text-gray-500`, `bg-white`, `border-neutral-200`) or hex/oklch literals. Every color rides a BoardUI semantic token, which also makes dark mode automatic.
- Text: `text-text-primary`, `text-text-secondary`, `text-text-tertiary`, `text-text-placeholder`, errors `text-text-error-primary`.
- Surfaces: `bg-background-primary-default`, `bg-background-secondary-default` / `-hover`, `bg-background-tertiary-default`, page ground `bg-background-full`.
- Borders: `border-border-button-default` / `-hover`, hairlines `border-separator-border`, tables `border-border-table`, errors `border-border-error-default`.
- Icons: `text-foreground-icon-primary` through `text-foreground-icon-quaternary`.
- Charts: the `chart-1` … `chart-5` tokens (plus `-active` variants). CTAs and selection states: the `accent-50` … `accent-950` ramp.
- Dark mode flips tokens via the `.dark` class on `<html>`. Do not write `dark:` overrides with raw colors; if a token pair looks wrong in dark mode, pick a different token, not a literal.

## Typography: composite utilities only

- Use BoardUI's composite type utilities: `text-title-1-medium`, `text-title-2-medium`, `text-title-3-semibold`, `text-headline-medium`, `text-body-medium`, `text-body-regular`, `text-body-2-*`, `text-caption-1-semibold`, and friends. Each sets size, weight, line-height, and letter-spacing together.
- Never rebuild type by stacking `text-sm font-medium leading-5`; if a style seems missing, look in `styles/typography.css` before inventing one.

## Spacing and shape

- Stay on Tailwind's spacing scale (`gap-2`, `p-4`, `mt-6`); prefer flex/grid `gap` over per-child margins. Arbitrary values (`p-[13px]`) only when matching an existing BoardUI component exactly.
- Cards and panels: `rounded-3xl` with `border-border-button-default`. Inputs and menu rows: `rounded-md` to `rounded-xl`. Pills: `rounded-full`.

## Mechanics

- Direction: wrap the app (or a mixed-language region) in `DirectionProvider` from `@/components/foundations/direction/direction`, with an explicit BCP 47 `locale` (`ar`, `he`, `en-US`, `zh-CN`). Set matching `lang` and `dir` on `<html>` for full-app RTL. CSS `dir` alone does not configure React Aria keyboard navigation or portal placement. Use `useDirection()` for custom interactions and put its value on custom portal roots.
- Use logical styles: `ms`/`me`, `ps`/`pe`, `start`/`end`, `text-start`/`text-end`, `border-s`/`border-e`, `rounded-s`/`rounded-e`, and inline logical CSS properties. Mirror navigation/disclosure glyphs and horizontal drawer motion in RTL. Preserve physical coordinates for measured geometry, charts, canvas, and decorative art. Keep code, OTP digits, email addresses and URLs in explicit LTR regions; isolate mixed text with `<bdi>` or `dir="auto"`. Translating labels and formatting application data is separate from layout direction. See https://www.boardui.com/rtl.

- Internal vertical scroll regions must soften the top edge with a progressive blur and surface fade once scrolled, rather than sharply clipping content. Keep headers outside the scroll region. Use a stationary, `pointer-events-none`, `aria-hidden` overlay in a relative wrapper: a 24px masked 1px backdrop blur, a 16px masked 4px backdrop blur, and a gradient from the enclosing semantic surface token to transparent. Ramp each layer's opacity from 0 to 1 over the first 24px of scrolling; keep it invisible at scrollTop 0. Apply opacity to the individual layers, never the overlay parent (a translucent parent creates a backdrop root and can break blur at normal browser zoom). Verify top/reset, overflow, light/dark mode, and 100% zoom; preserve keyboard scrolling and do not blur the whole content area.

- Merge classes with `cx()` from `@/utils/cx` (tailwind-merge aware of BoardUI's composite text styles). No string concatenation, no plain `clsx`.
- Icons come from `@remixicon/react`, passed as component references (`leadingIcon={RiAddLine}`), not rendered elements.
- Form components build on `react-aria-components`; extend the installed BoardUI form components rather than raw `<input>`/`<select>`.
- Focus states: `outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-border-focus-ring`.

When unsure about a token, a component's API, or working example code, ask the BoardUI MCP server: `get_theme`, `get_component`, `get_usage_examples`.
<!-- boardui:rules:end -->

right; the three token-budget signatures are the weak spot.

- Budget signatures remain unreliable: every token regression (R1 tool schema, R2 search_help rule) inflates every category, so a

  order_status-specific regression is earlier; reverting 59c8b10 left tokens above the limit (revert test failed, flagged
  "multiple regressions likely"). refund_outside_policy landed on an unrelated later commit (5cee99b) with an inconclusive revert.
  refund_within_policy matches the key only because 59c8b10 is a contributor; its revert test also failed (0/3 -> 0/3).
- Smart was slower than plain on the two budget signatures that needed many rounds (+12, +6 rounds); it won on the two behavioural ones
  (-6, -1) and tied on one. Planner context 20-24k tokens with the graph vs 43-47k reading the raw range.

/**
 * Figma source: Board UI → Buttons (node 3656:13819).
 *
 * Variant matrix from Figma:
 *   Type     = Primary | Secondary | Ghost | Danger
 *   Size     = Medium  | Small | Xs
 *   State    = Default | Hover | Active | Disabled        (CSS pseudo)
 *   OnlyIcon = false   | true
 *
 * Sizing (1:1 with Figma):
 *
 *                       Medium                    Small                     Xs
 *   container          h=36, p=8,   r=10         h=32, px=8 py=6, r=8      h=24, px=8, r=4
 *   gap                 2px                       2px                      1.33px→1
 *   icon                20×20                     18×18                    14×14
 *   label wrapper       px=4                      px=2                     px=2
 *   text style          Body 1/Medium             Body 1/Medium            Caption 1/Semibold
 *   icon-only square    36×36 (content-derived)   32×32 (forced size)      24×24 (forced size)
 *
 * `xs` is the smallest tier — first needed for the calendar template's
 * event-details modal ("Join" / edit-icon buttons, node 3920:10954), which
 * scales every dimension down by the same ~0.667 factor from Figma; the
 * table above rounds those to clean pixel values rather than reproducing
 * the fractional source numbers.
 *
 * Icons are rendered by the component itself via the `leadingIcon` /
 * `trailingIcon` props so the consumer can't pass the wrong size. Pass
 * a Remix Icon component reference (`RiAddLine`, not `<RiAddLine />`).
 *
 * For icon-only buttons:
 *   <Button iconOnly leadingIcon={RiAddLine} aria-label="Add" />
 *
 * The HTML `type` prop is preserved; Figma's "Type" enum is renamed to
 * `variant` to avoid the clash.
 */

type ButtonVariant = "primary" | "secondary" | "ghost" | "danger";
type ButtonSize = "medium" | "small" | "xs";

type IconComponent = ComponentType<{
  className?: string;
  "aria-hidden"?: boolean | "true" | "false";
}>;

export interface ButtonProps
  extends Omit<ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>, "children"> {
  variant?: ButtonVariant;
  size?: ButtonSize;
  iconOnly?: boolean;
  leadingIcon?: IconComponent;
  trailingIcon?: IconComponent;
  children?: ReactNode;
  ref?: Ref<HTMLButtonElement>;
}

export interface ButtonLinkProps
  extends Omit<AnchorHTMLAttributes<HTMLAnchorElement>, "children"> {
  variant?: ButtonVariant;
  size?: ButtonSize;
  iconOnly?: boolean;
  leadingIcon?: IconComponent;
  trailingIcon?: IconComponent;
  children?: ReactNode;

}
```
